Deploying with Hardhat

Configure networks, secure keys, script deployments with ethers.js, and troubleshoot deploy-time errors so you can move from local tests to Sepolia or Mainnet safely.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this set of objectives you will find four concrete outcomes that guide the hands-on work. First, you'll configure a Hardhat project so it targets local, testnet, and Mainnet networks with the correct RPC endpoints and chain IDs. That matters because a misconfigured network causes signing and broadcast failures. Second, you'll write and run deployment scripts using ethers. js. You will learn how ContractFactory compiles, deploys, waits for confirmation, and returns a usable contract object for immediate interaction. Third, you'll manage secrets by using environment variables: storing RPC URLs, private keys, and A P I keys in a. env file and excluding it from source control prevents accidental leaks. Fourth, you'll learn practical troubleshooting steps for common Hardhat errors like insufficient funds, constructor reverts, RPC timeouts, and chain ID mismatches. Each objective maps to a verified action you can perform in a terminal and code editor, and together they let you reliably move from local tests to public testnets.

screens.title: What is Hardhat and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat is a developer-focused environment that combines compilation, testing, local networking, and extensibility via plugins. Its built-in Hardhat Network gives you a fast, local Ethereum node for iterative development, letting you deploy and test contracts in seconds without paying gas. The power of Hardhat becomes evident when you script deployments: rather than manually sending transactions, you write JS scripts that call ethers. getContractFactory and deploy contract instances programmatically. This yields repeatable, version-controlled deploy steps. A concrete example is compiling a Greeter contract and deploying it to the Hardhat Network for rapid validation. A common misconception is that Hardhat only runs locally; in fact, it is used to orchestrate deployments to public networks through RPC configuration in hardhat. config. js. Why this matters: using Hardhat centralizes build and deployment steps, integrates with tools like etherscan verification and gas reporting, and supports automation through custom tasks. As you progress, think about how scripting deployments reduces human error and enables CI/CD pipelines for blockchain projects. What is Hardhat and why it matters means hardhat is a flexible environment that runs a local chain, compiles contracts, and provides a scripting surface for automated deployments.. In practical terms, a development environment, local network, and plugin ecosystem. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › What is Hardhat
Quick definition

Hardhat is a development environment with a local network, scriptable tasks, and a plugin system that supports deployments to real networks via RPC.

Local network
Hardhat Network runs locally for quick compile-deploy-test cycles, replacing slow public networks during development.
Scripting
You write Node scripts that use ethers.js to deploy and interact with contracts deterministically.
Plugins
Toolbox plugins add verification, gas reporting, and testing support to standardize workflows.
Concrete example
Compile Greeter, deploy to Hardhat Network, and call greet() to validate behavior before moving to Sepolia.
Common misconception

Some learners assume Hardhat is only for local testing. In practice you configure RPC endpoints in hardhat.config.js to run the same scripts against Sepolia or Mainnet.

Key Takeaway

Hardhat is the scripting backbone for reliable, repeatable contract deployment and management.

screens.title: Understanding hardhat.config.js
screens.narratorSegment: hardhat. config. js is the single source of configuration for a Hardhat project. It declares the Solidity compiler version, network endpoints and accounts, and plugin settings such as etherscan and gas reporter. When you run a deployment script, Hardhat consults this file to determine whether to compile, which network to use, and how to sign transactions. A concrete example from the lesson content shows settings for Sepolia and Mainnet with RPC URLs read from process. env, the PRIVATE_KEY supplied as an accounts array, and explicit chainId entries. The reason this matters is that mismatched chainId or missing accounts will cause signing errors or silent failures. A common mistake is hardcoding secrets directly in this file; instead, load them from a. env with require('dotenv'). config(). When you add plugins like @nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox, the config file also toggles verification and gas reporting. Review and test your hardhat. config. js before running deployment scripts to avoid costly mistakes when you move from Sepolia to Mainnet. Understanding hardhat.config.js means use hardhat.config.js to declare compilers, networks, accounts, plugins, and to safely reference environment variables.. In practical terms, where compiler versions, networks, and plugins live. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use hardhat.config.js to declare compilers, networks, accounts, plugins, and to safely reference environment variables.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › hardhat.config.js
Core fields
  • solidity: compiler version for contracts
  • networks: named networks with url, accounts and chainId
  • etherscan: apiKey for verifying contracts
  • gasReporter: plugin configuration for cost estimation
Best practice

Load secrets via process.env with require('dotenv').config() and keep your .env in .gitignore to avoid leaking keys.

Example snippet
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox");
require("dotenv").config();

const SEPOLIA_RPC_URL = process.env.SEPOLIA_RPC_URL;
const PRIVATE_KEY = process.env.PRIVATE_KEY;

module.exports = {
  solidity: "0.8.20",
  networks: {
    sepolia: { url: SEPOLIA_RPC_URL, accounts: PRIVATE_KEY ? [PRIVATE_KEY] : [], chainId: 11155111 }
  },
  etherscan: { apiKey: process.env.ETHERSCAN_API_KEY }
};
Common mistake

Hardcoding a PRIVATE_KEY in the config exposes funds. Always use environment variables.

screens.title: Environment variables and .env security
screens.narratorSegment: Keeping secrets out of your repository is essential. Hardhat projects should read RPC URLs and private keys from environment variables via require('dotenv'). config(). The typical pattern is to create a. env file at the project root with keys like SEPOLIA_RPC_URL, MAINNET_RPC_URL, PRIVATE_KEY, and ETHERSCAN_API_KEY, then add. env to. gitignore. A concrete example: set SEPOLIA_RPC_URL to your Alchemy or Infura endpoint and PRIVATE_KEY to your deployer key. When you run Node scripts, hardhat. config. js accesses process. env. SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and process. env. PRIVATE_KEY so no secret is committed. A common misconception is that. env files are private by default — they are only private if you prevent them from being checked in. Treat every private key like a real wallet: if it appears in source, rotate keys and consider the repository compromised. Also avoid printing the full private key in logs. When using CI/CD, set environment variables in the pipeline configuration rather than committing. env. This practice allows safe deployment scripts and repeatable builds across machines without exposing credentials. Environment variables and .env security means never hardcode secrets; use .env and ci pipeline environment variables and keep .env out of source control.. In practical terms, safely store rpc urls, private keys, and api keys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Configuring networks (Sepolia & Mainnet)
screens.narratorSegment: Network configuration tells Hardhat how to reach a blockchain and which account will pay gas. In hardhat. config. js you declare named networks such as sepolia and mainnet with a URL, accounts array, and chainId. The lesson example shows using SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and MAINNET_RPC_URL from process. env and adding PRIVATE_KEY as the single signer. The chainId is important: Sepolia uses 11155111 and Mainnet uses 1; a mismatch can cause transaction signing errors because signatures include chain identifiers. When deploying to a public testnet, ensure your RPC provider (Alchemy, Infura, or another node) is responsive and that your deployer account is funded with test ETH. If you need custom gas settings, you can add gasPrice, maxFeePerGas, or maxPriorityFeePerGas either in the network config or per-transaction options in your deployment script. Remember that local Hardhat Network requires no external RPC and often provides unlocked accounts for convenience; public networks require explicit private-key-based accounts. Test your configuration by running a simple script with --network sepolia and observing whether the deploy transaction is constructed and broadcast successfully. Configuring networks (Sepolia & Mainnet) means correct urls, accounts, and chainid are required to sign and broadcast transactions to the intended network.. In practical terms, set rpc urls, accounts, and chainid correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Essential fields

screens.title: Deploying a contract with ContractFactory
screens.narratorSegment: ContractFactory is the ethers. js abstraction used to deploy new smart contracts. In a typical Hardhat script you first call ethers. getSigners() to get the deployer account, then use ethers. getContractFactory('ContractName') to obtain a factory for your compiled contract. Calling. deploy(...) on that factory sends a transaction that creates the contract on-chain. After calling. deploy(), await greeter. deployed() to wait for confirmations and obtain the contract address. The lesson's Greeter script demonstrates these steps and then immediately interacts with the deployed contract using greet() and setGreeting(). A concrete example: the script prints the deployer address and balance, deploys Greeter with an initial message, reads the greeting, sets a new greeting, waits for the transaction to be mined, and reads the updated greeting. A common misconception is that. deploy() returns a fully settled contract immediately; in reality you should await the deployed() promise and optionally tx. wait() for state-changing calls. This sequence guarantees your script knows the final on-chain state and can continue with verification or post-deploy tasks. Deploying a contract with ContractFactory means use getcontractfactory, deploy, await deployed(), and tx.wait() to ensure contracts are published and state changes are confirmed.. In practical terms, walkthrough of a deploy script using ethers.js. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use getContractFactory, deploy, await deployed(), and tx.wait() to ensure contracts are published and state changes are confirmed.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › ContractFactory deploy
Key steps
  1. Get signer: const [deployer] = await ethers.getSigners()
  2. Get factory: const Greeter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Greeter")
  3. Deploy: const greeter = await Greeter.deploy("Hello")
  4. Await: await greeter.deployed()
Why await deployed()

Awaiting ensures the deployment transaction is mined and you have a valid contract address you can attach to or interact with immediately.

Example script
// scripts/deployGreeter.js
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const [deployer] = await ethers.getSigners();
  console.log("Deploying with:", deployer.address);

  const Greeter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Greeter");
  const greeter = await Greeter.deploy("Hello, Cohortia!");
  await greeter.deployed();
  console.log("Greeter deployed to:", greeter.address);
}

main().catch((e)=>{console.error(e);process.exit(1);});
Key Takeaway

Deployments are programmatic and should await confirmations to be deterministic.

screens.title: Interacting with deployed contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Once a contract is deployed you can interact with it immediately through the returned contract object or by attaching to an existing address. Ethers. js exposes getContractAt(name, address) and ContractFactory. attach(address) for this purpose. The lesson's Greeter example first calls greeter. greet() to read state, then calls greeter. setGreeting(newMessage) to create a state-changing transaction. Important details: after sending a transaction you should call tx. wait() to ensure the change is mined before reading the updated state. A concrete scenario: deploy a Greeter, call greet() to confirm the initial message, setGreeting("Welcome to Web3 Development!"), wait for tx. wait(), then call greet() again to confirm the update. A common misconception is treating tx sending as synchronous; in reality you are creating a pending transaction that needs to be mined. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Interacting post-deploy
Read vs Write

Read-only calls (view) return data immediately. State-changing calls produce transactions that must be mined.

Pattern
  1. Call view functions directly: await contract.greet()
  2. Send state-change: const tx = await contract.setGreeting("...")
  3. Await mining: await tx.wait()
  4. Confirm state: await contract.greet()
Attach to existing contract
// Using getContractAt
const SimpleStorage = await ethers.getContractAt("SimpleStorage", "0x...address...");
const tx = await SimpleStorage.set(123);
await tx.wait();
console.log((await SimpleStorage.get()).toString());
Misconception

Do not assume a sent transaction has changed state until you call tx.wait(); otherwise your script may read the old value.

screens.narratorSegment: To run a deployment script against a network configured in hardhat. config. js you use the --network flag. For example: npx hardhat run scripts/deployGreeter. js --network sepolia. This tells Hardhat to use the sepolia configuration, including RPC URL and accounts, to compile and broadcast transactions. screens.title: Common deployment error: insufficient funds
screens.narratorSegment: The error 'sender doesn't have enough funds to send tx' is one of the most frequent deployment blockers. It means the account associated with your PRIVATE_KEY lacks enough ETH to cover the gas cost of the deploy transaction. Diagnosis starts by printing the deployer address and balance in your script; this gives you a public address to paste into a faucet if you are on Sepolia. The resolution is straightforward for testnets: obtain test ETH from a Sepolia faucet and retry. For Mainnet, you must send real ETH to that address, which highlights why testing on Sepolia is essential before Mainnet. A subtle troubleshooting step: ensure the PRIVATE_KEY in your. env actually corresponds to the expected public address; a typo can mean you're funding the wrong account. Finally, when funding and retrying, be mindful of nonce gaps if previous transactions are pending. Keeping an eye on the explorer for the deployer address speeds resolution and prevents wasted retries. Reflect: always verify the account and balance before sending a costly deploy transaction. Common deployment error: insufficient funds means check deployer.getbalance(), fund the correct public address from a faucet on testnets, and confirm the private_key corresponds to the funded address.. Diagnosis steps
  1. Print deployer address and balance in your script

  3. Check pending transactions or nonce issues in the explorer

Request test ETH for Sepolia or send ETH for Mainnet. Confirm balance before redeploying.

Example terminal tip
console.log("Account balance:", (await deployer.getBalance()).toString())
If this prints a low value, the deploy will fail. Fund the printed address via a faucet and try again.

screens.title: Other common errors and fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond funding errors, Hardhat deployments often hit three other classes of problems. First, constructor errors — shown as 'missing revert data' or 'VM Exception while processing transaction: revert' — usually indicate incorrect constructor arguments or logic that reverts because of invalid inputs. The fix is to verify constructor parameters and initial state assumptions. Second, 'Transaction was not mined within 750 seconds' signals that the transaction did not get included in a block. This can occur from very low gas settings, high network congestion, or an unstable RPC provider. Remedies include increasing gasPrice or maxFeePerGas/maxPriorityFeePerGas in your transaction options or switching RPC providers. Third, incorrect chainId causes signing errors because signatures include the network chain identifier; ensure the chainId in hardhat. config. js matches the target network. A common diagnostic strategy is to reproduce the deployment on a local Hardhat Network to verify contract logic, then test on Sepolia with known-good parameters, increasing gas limits when the network is congested. These steps let you triage whether an error is about code, gas, or connectivity. Other common errors and fixes means distinguish constructor logic errors from gas/timeouts and chainid mismatches; test locally, then adjust params when targeting remote networks.. In practical terms, constructor reverts, timeouts, and chainid mismatches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. screens.title: Hardhat tasks for contract management
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat tasks let you define reusable command-line actions for things like updating contract state without redeploying. A task is a small JavaScript function declared in hardhat. config. js or a separate tasks/ file and registered with task(name, description). addParam(...). setAction(async taskArgs => {... }). The lesson includes a task example called set-greeting that attaches to an existing Greeter contract and calls setGreeting with a provided argument. Running npx hardhat set-greeting --contract 0x... --newgreeting "Hello" --network sepolia executes the task. Tasks are helpful for maintenance operations, migrations, or scripted administrative actions and can be included in CI pipelines. A misconception is using tasks as a substitute for proper access control; tasks should act through the same policy and private keys as other scripts. When building tasks, validate inputs and wait for tx. wait() to ensure the action completes before exiting. Tasks make routine management predictable and reduce manual terminal commands during operations. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Hardhat tasks
Why tasks?
  • Automate routine post-deploy actions
  • Run admin calls with a single command
  • Integrate maintenance into CI pipelines
Task example
task("set-greeting", "Sets a new greeting on the Greeter contract")
  .addParam("contract", "The Greeter contract address")
  .addParam("newgreeting", "The new greeting message")
  .setAction(async (taskArgs) => {
    const Greeter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Greeter");
    const greeter = Greeter.attach(taskArgs.contract);
    const tx = await greeter.setGreeting(taskArgs.newgreeting);
    await tx.wait();
    console.log(`Greeting set to "${taskArgs.newgreeting}" on ${taskArgs.contract}`);
  });
Key Takeaway

Define tasks for repeatable management and include validation to avoid accidental state changes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › ERC-20 deployment
MyToken.sol (contract)
// contracts/MyToken.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/ERC20.sol";

contract MyToken is ERC20 {
  constructor(string memory name, string memory symbol, uint256 initialSupply) ERC20(name, symbol) {
    _mint(msg.sender, initialSupply);
  }
}
Note: initialSupply should be parsed with 18 decimals in your script to match ERC-20 units.
deployMyToken.js (script)
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const [deployer] = await ethers.getSigners();
  const initialSupply = ethers.utils.parseUnits("1000000", 18);
  const MyToken = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyToken");
  const myToken = await MyToken.deploy("Cohortia Token", "CHT", initialSupply);
  await myToken.deployed();
  console.log("MyToken deployed to:", myToken.address);
}

main().catch((e)=>{console.error(e);process.exit(1);});
Checklist

Install OpenZeppelin, populate .env, fund deployer on Sepolia, run npx hardhat run scripts/deployMyToken.js --network sepolia.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how Hardhat takes the pain out of deploying smart contracts. We start by configuring hardhat. config. js with compiler and network settings, then we secure A P I and private keys with environment variables. You will see how ethers. js integrates with Hardhat via ContractFactory to compile, deploy, and interact with contracts programmatically. We will walk through a complete deploy script that deploys a Greeter contract, confirms deployment, calls its read functions, and updates state with a signed transaction. Along the way I will highlight common deployment failures — insufficient funds, constructor errors that revert, timeouts from RPC providers, and chain ID mismatches — and show practical fixes you can apply in real projects. Finally, we'll discuss tasks for post-deployment management and a hands-on ERC-20 deployment to Sepolia that ties the whole flow together. By the end you should be able to configure a project, run a deployment safely, and verify your deployed contract. Think about which network you will target first and which safeguards you will add to your workflow.

In this set of objectives you will find four concrete outcomes that guide the hands-on work. First, you'll configure a Hardhat project so it targets local, testnet, and Mainnet networks with the correct RPC endpoints and chain IDs. That matters because a misconfigured network causes signing and broadcast failures. Second, you'll write and run deployment scripts using ethers. js. You will learn how ContractFactory compiles, deploys, waits for confirmation, and returns a usable contract object for immediate interaction. Third, you'll manage secrets by using environment variables: storing RPC URLs, private keys, and A P I keys in a. env file and excluding it from source control prevents accidental leaks. Fourth, you'll learn practical troubleshooting steps for common Hardhat errors like insufficient funds, constructor reverts, RPC timeouts, and chain ID mismatches. Each objective maps to a verified action you can perform in a terminal and code editor, and together they let you reliably move from local tests to public testnets.

These objectives extend the basics into practical application. You will apply configuration skills to run scripts against Sepolia and verify that deployed addresses appear on a block explorer. You will also create and run Hardhat tasks for routine actions, such as updating contract state without redeploying. These tasks demonstrate how Hardhat can become part of your automation pipeline. Finally you will be able to reason about gas and use the gas reporter to estimate costs before a Mainnet deploy. Together these outcomes let you not only deploy but manage contracts across their lifecycle: deploy, verify, update via tasks, and monitor gas impact. A short mental check: if you can configure networks, deploy a contract, call a function remotely, and run a task that touches the same contract, you have mastered the deployment cycle this chapter teaches.

Hardhat is a developer-focused environment that combines compilation, testing, local networking, and extensibility via plugins. Its built-in Hardhat Network gives you a fast, local Ethereum node for iterative development, letting you deploy and test contracts in seconds without paying gas. The power of Hardhat becomes evident when you script deployments: rather than manually sending transactions, you write JS scripts that call ethers. getContractFactory and deploy contract instances programmatically. This yields repeatable, version-controlled deploy steps. A concrete example is compiling a Greeter contract and deploying it to the Hardhat Network for rapid validation. A common misconception is that Hardhat only runs locally; in fact, it is used to orchestrate deployments to public networks through RPC configuration in hardhat. config. js. Why this matters: using Hardhat centralizes build and deployment steps, integrates with tools like etherscan verification and gas reporting, and supports automation through custom tasks. hardhat. config. js is the single source of configuration for a Hardhat project. It declares the Solidity compiler version, network endpoints and accounts, and plugin settings such as etherscan and gas reporter. When you run a deployment script, Hardhat consults this file to determine whether to compile, which network to use, and how to sign transactions. A concrete example from the lesson content shows settings for Sepolia and Mainnet with RPC URLs read from process. env, the PRIVATE_KEY supplied as an accounts array, and explicit chainId entries. The reason this matters is that mismatched chainId or missing accounts will cause signing errors or silent failures. A common mistake is hardcoding secrets directly in this file; instead, load them from a. env with require('dotenv'). config(). When you add plugins like @nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox, the config file also toggles verification and gas reporting. Review and test your hardhat. config. js before running deployment scripts to avoid costly mistakes when you move from Sepolia to Mainnet. Keeping secrets out of your repository is essential. Hardhat projects should read RPC URLs and private keys from environment variables via require('dotenv'). config(). The typical pattern is to create a. env file at the project root with keys like SEPOLIA_RPC_URL, MAINNET_RPC_URL, PRIVATE_KEY, and ETHERSCAN_API_KEY, then add. env to. gitignore. A concrete example: set SEPOLIA_RPC_URL to your Alchemy or Infura endpoint and PRIVATE_KEY to your deployer key. When you run Node scripts, hardhat. config. js accesses process. env. SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and process. env. PRIVATE_KEY so no secret is committed. A common misconception is that. env files are private by default — they are only private if you prevent them from being checked in. Treat every private key like a real wallet: if it appears in source, rotate keys and consider the repository compromised. Also avoid printing the full private key in logs. When using CI/CD, set environment variables in the pipeline configuration rather than committing. env. This practice allows safe deployment scripts and repeatable builds across machines without exposing credentials. Network configuration tells Hardhat how to reach a blockchain and which account will pay gas. In hardhat. config. js you declare named networks such as sepolia and mainnet with a URL, accounts array, and chainId. The lesson example shows using SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and MAINNET_RPC_URL from process. env and adding PRIVATE_KEY as the single signer. The chainId is important: Sepolia uses 11155111 and Mainnet uses 1; a mismatch can cause transaction signing errors because signatures include chain identifiers. When deploying to a public testnet, ensure your RPC provider (Alchemy, Infura, or another node) is responsive and that your deployer account is funded with test ETH. If you need custom gas settings, you can add gasPrice, maxFeePerGas, or maxPriorityFeePerGas either in the network config or per-transaction options in your deployment script. Remember that local Hardhat Network requires no external RPC and often provides unlocked accounts for convenience; public networks require explicit private-key-based accounts. Test your configuration by running a simple script with --network sepolia and observing whether the deploy transaction is constructed and broadcast successfully. ContractFactory is the ethers. js abstraction used to deploy new smart contracts. In a typical Hardhat script you first call ethers. getSigners() to get the deployer account, then use ethers. getContractFactory('ContractName') to obtain a factory for your compiled contract. Calling. deploy(...) on that factory sends a transaction that creates the contract on-chain. After calling. deploy(), await greeter. deployed() to wait for confirmations and obtain the contract address. The lesson's Greeter script demonstrates these steps and then immediately interacts with the deployed contract using greet() and setGreeting(). A concrete example: the script prints the deployer address and balance, deploys Greeter with an initial message, reads the greeting, sets a new greeting, waits for the transaction to be mined, and reads the updated greeting. A common misconception is that. deploy() returns a fully settled contract immediately; in reality you should await the deployed() promise and optionally tx. wait() for state-changing calls. This sequence guarantees your script knows the final on-chain state and can continue with verification or post-deploy tasks. Deploying a contract with ContractFactory means use getcontractfactory, deploy, await deployed(), and tx.wait() to ensure contracts are published and state changes are confirmed.. To run a deployment script against a network configured in hardhat. config. js you use the --network flag. For example: npx hardhat run scripts/deployGreeter. js --network sepolia. This tells Hardhat to use the sepolia configuration, including RPC URL and accounts, to compile and broadcast transactions. Running without a --network flag defaults to the Hardhat Network. A practical tip: print the deployer address and balance at the start of your script so you can verify the account and funding before continuing. If the deployer has insufficient funds, you will see an error complaining about the sender's balance. When working in CI, set environment variables for RPC URLs and keys in the pipeline configuration and invoke the same command to ensure consistent behavior. If a transaction stalls, examine your RPC provider health or increase gas settings; you can also try switching providers if you suspect rate-limiting. Use this flag consistently so your scripts remain portable between local tests and remote testnets or Mainnet. The error 'sender doesn't have enough funds to send tx' is one of the most frequent deployment blockers. It means the account associated with your PRIVATE_KEY lacks enough ETH to cover the gas cost of the deploy transaction. Diagnosis starts by printing the deployer address and balance in your script; this gives you a public address to paste into a faucet if you are on Sepolia. The resolution is straightforward for testnets: obtain test ETH from a Sepolia faucet and retry. For Mainnet, you must send real ETH to that address, which highlights why testing on Sepolia is essential before Mainnet. A subtle troubleshooting step: ensure the PRIVATE_KEY in your. env actually corresponds to the expected public address; a typo can mean you're funding the wrong account. Finally, when funding and retrying, be mindful of nonce gaps if previous transactions are pending. Keeping an eye on the explorer for the deployer address speeds resolution and prevents wasted retries. Reflect: always verify the account and balance before sending a costly deploy transaction. Beyond funding errors, Hardhat deployments often hit three other classes of problems. First, constructor errors — shown as 'missing revert data' or 'VM Exception while processing transaction: revert' — usually indicate incorrect constructor arguments or logic that reverts because of invalid inputs. The fix is to verify constructor parameters and initial state assumptions. Second, 'Transaction was not mined within 750 seconds' signals that the transaction did not get included in a block. This can occur from very low gas settings, high network congestion, or an unstable RPC provider. Remedies include increasing gasPrice or maxFeePerGas/maxPriorityFeePerGas in your transaction options or switching RPC providers. Third, incorrect chainId causes signing errors because signatures include the network chain identifier; ensure the chainId in hardhat. config. js matches the target network. A common diagnostic strategy is to reproduce the deployment on a local Hardhat Network to verify contract logic, then test on Sepolia with known-good parameters, increasing gas limits when the network is congested. These steps let you triage whether an error is about code, gas, or connectivity. Other common errors and fixes means distinguish constructor logic errors from gas/timeouts and chainid mismatches; test locally, then adjust params when targeting remote networks.. Hardhat tasks let you define reusable command-line actions for things like updating contract state without redeploying. A task is a small JavaScript function declared in hardhat. config. js or a separate tasks/ file and registered with task(name, description). addParam(...). setAction(async taskArgs => {... }). The lesson includes a task example called set-greeting that attaches to an existing Greeter contract and calls setGreeting with a provided argument. Running npx hardhat set-greeting --contract 0x... --newgreeting "Hello" --network sepolia executes the task. Tasks are helpful for maintenance operations, migrations, or scripted administrative actions and can be included in CI pipelines. A misconception is using tasks as a substitute for proper access control; tasks should act through the same policy and private keys as other scripts. When building tasks, validate inputs and wait for tx. wait() to ensure the action completes before exiting. Tasks make routine management predictable and reduce manual terminal commands during operations. Let's summarize the core concepts you should carry forward. First, hardhat. config. js is the authoritative place for compiler, network, and plugin settings; always load secrets from environment variables rather than hardcoding them. Second, ethers. js ContractFactory is the deploy-time abstraction you will use to compile and publish contracts; always await deployed() and tx. wait() when changing state. Third, common deployment errors fall into funding, constructor logic, gas/timeouts, and chainId mismatches — triage these by checking balances, reproducing locally, and adjusting gas or providers. Finally, Hardhat tasks let you automate management tasks after deployment. Keep. env out of source control and verify deployed addresses on the block explorer as a final confirmation step. These concise checks form a practical checklist for any production-ready deployment flow.
